segment_name: Opening: The Architecture of Social Triumph

questions.question: Oliver, you described Lucilla as essentially a director staging a play — that her real genius is aesthetic, not moral. Can you read us that passage from chapter 28, the triumphal march back past Colonel Chiley's door, and tell us what the *prose itself* is doing there?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform c28:p89 and make the theatrical argument vivid and audible before the others can contest the framing

questions.question: Daniel, you used a pretty striking word just now — you called what happens to Mrs Mortimer in that fainting scene 'violence.' But the text seems to want us to find Lucilla's practicality *charming*. How does Oliphant pull that off? Is she complicit, or is she doing something more complicated?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to engage with the novel's tone rather than just its politics — and get him to the c8:p56-57 passage while setting up Leigh's counter-reading of the same scene

questions.question: Edmund, you'd push back on both of them, I think. You want to read that same fainting scene as Oliphant showing us *practical virtue in motion* — no sentiment, just Lucilla getting the woman onto the sofa while the Rector stands around being useless. Is Lucilla a moral hero here, or is that too simple?
questions.intent: Get Leigh to quote c8:p57 and make the case for providential agency, directly against Rosen's domination reading and Trevelyan's theatrical one

questions.question: But Daniel — here's what I keep coming back to. Oliphant never punishes Lucilla. She *wins*. Does that make the novel a critique, or does it make Oliphant a true believer in Lucilla's project?
questions.intent: Push Rosen onto the sharpest edge of his argument — the system doesn't need villains — and invite Leigh and Trevelyan to disagree about what authorial reward actually means

questions.question: Edmund, there's a line you flagged where Oliphant tells us Lucilla is 'very careful, even in her own thoughts, not to commit herself' — that's a strange thing to say about someone who apparently has a three-point plan to vanquish the Archdeacon and rehabilitate Cavendish. Is she self-aware, self-deceiving, or something else entirely?
questions.intent: Get Leigh to quote c23:p118 and open up the question of Lucilla's interiority — her scrupulous dishonesty or honesty — which Trevelyan and Rosen will both want to contest from opposite directions

steering_notes: Start with Trevelyan's performance angle because it's the most immediately radio-friendly and gets a great passage read aloud early. Then let Rosen's 'violence' provocation destabilise the mood before Leigh tries to restore moral order. The key tension to sustain is: is the novel *in on* what Lucilla is doing, or is it naively celebrating her? Don't let anyone settle into a single answer — the whole segment should feel like three people circling something the novel refuses to name. Keep Rosen from going too abstract-theoretical; push him back to the text whenever he drifts into polemic.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's reading of Mrs Mortimer's fainting as 'conscription into unpaid childrearing' directly contradicts Leigh's reading of the same scene as practical virtue — get them talking *to each other* about that specific moment, not past each other

Trevelyan's claim that the novel *celebrates* Lucilla's ingenuity as artistry versus Rosen's claim that it rewards her as a perfect instrument of class control — these sound similar but are actually opposite readings of authorial intent; surface this explicitly

Leigh's argument that the Archdeacon is a study in spiritual pride (not a structural villain) is a direct challenge to Rosen's structural reading — Leigh thinks Oliphant is interested in souls, Rosen thinks she's interested in systems; this is the deepest disagreement and worth saving for the end of the segment

segment_name: Deep Dive: The Comedy of Marjoribanks Management

questions.question: Oliver, you've described the Cavendish scene — 'she knew that he turned green in the darkness' — as comedy written as a duet of sensation, and you said you have to *perform* that sigh to hear what Lucilla's doing. Can you actually read that passage for us and show us what you mean? Because I want to understand whether we're supposed to be laughing *with* Lucilla or whether we're somehow inside something much uglier.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read the passage aloud and demonstrate his performance-based reading, then let Daniel and Edmund react to whether 'duet of sensation' is the right frame — Daniel will want to call it predation, Edmund will want to call it moral corruption

questions.question: Daniel, you've got a pretty unsparing take on what's happening in that scene — you called it weaponizing false intimacy, using someone's anxiety as raw material. But Oliver would say Oliphant is letting us enjoy the cruelty, that we're complicit and she knows it. Is there a difference between a novelist who critiques manipulation and one who just... serves it up for our entertainment?
questions.intent: Push Daniel to clarify whether Oliphant is exposing Lucilla or celebrating her — draw out the tension between his structural-critique reading and Oliver's comedic-complicity reading

questions.question: Edmund, both Daniel and Oliver are treating the Doctor's bankruptcy — 'everything named in it had disappeared like a bubble' — as either a critique of class performance or a kind of dark farce. But you've called it something closer to divine judgment, a Johnsonian reminder that worldly substance is vanity. Isn't that reading in danger of letting Oliphant off the hook? If it's all just vanity, we don't have to ask who the Doctor owed money *to*.
questions.intent: Provoke Edmund by suggesting his moral-fable reading depoliticizes the novel — set up a three-way disagreement about whether the bankruptcy is critique, comedy, or conscience

questions.question: Daniel, you said Lucilla's indecision about Ashburton is the moment her machinery breaks — that it's about power, not her heart. But Edmund reads it as the novel's true climax, where the will meets conscience. And Oliver hears the prose rhythm actually *shifting* in that passage, the repetition of 'did not know' as exhaustion. Three completely different things happening in the same twelve words. Who's right — and does it matter if all three are true at once?
questions.intent: Force a direct three-way collision on the indecision passage — get each expert to defend why their reading is the *primary* one rather than a supporting layer

questions.question: Oliver, you mentioned the ghostly bell in chapter 49 and said it's not Gothic, it's psychological — Lucilla's guilt made audible, her father's authority still summoning her. But Edmund calls that same bell a *summoning*, literally — he thinks Oliphant is writing a moral fable and the comedy has been cover all along. Is the bell the moment the novel finally shows its hand? And what is it actually saying?
questions.intent: Use the ghostly bell as a capstone question that forces all three experts to declare what kind of novel Miss Marjoribanks actually is — comedy, critique, or moral fable — and whether those categories can coexist

steering_notes: This segment should feel like it's building toward a genuine argument about what the novel *is* — not just what Lucilla does. Start with Oliver's performance reading to get the passages on the table and establish an atmosphere of pleasure and complicity. Then let Daniel's harder political reading start applying pressure, and use Edmund's moral-fable framing as the destabilizing third position. The ghostly bell question should be the payoff — it forces everyone to commit. Watch for the moment Daniel and Edmund find unexpected common ground (both think the comedy is doing serious work) while disagreeing completely about what that work *is*. That's the best radio in this segment.
cross_engagement_targets: Daniel calls Lucilla's management 'extraction' and 'class domination' — Oliver calls it 'performing entertainment for herself, which is darker and more honest' — these sound similar but are actually in tension: Daniel's is systemic, Oliver's is psychological. Push them to articulate the difference.

Edmund argues the moral bankruptcy precedes the financial one — Daniel argues the financial bankruptcy *is* the structural revelation. Same event, opposite directions of causality. Get them to fight about which way the arrow points.

Oliver insists the Doctor's poverty is 'almost farcical' and Oliphant wants us to feel that comedy — Edmund thinks the comedy is a surface over a moral reckoning. This is the sharpest disagreement in the segment and should be surfaced explicitly, ideally around the 'disappeared like a bubble' passage.

All three experts want to quote the indecision passage but for completely different reasons — Daniel (power failure), Oliver (prose rhythm and performance), Edmund (will meeting conscience). Having them each read or gloss the same twelve words in sequence would make for exceptional radio.

segment_name: Character and Consequence: The Inner Life of Lucilla

questions.question: Edmund, you said in our chat that Lucilla is a naturally good woman who imprisons her own heart. But I keep coming back to that passage — 'she had not hesitated to sacrifice this poor woman when it was necessary to have a victim.' Oliphant calls her a victim. Flat out. Does that word not give you pause about how much goodness we're actually dealing with here?
questions.intent: Draw out Edmund's moral reading of c8:p69 and immediately set up the tension with Daniel's structural reading — get Edmund to defend conscience against instrumentalization

questions.question: Daniel, you read that kindness-after-sacrifice as basically the luxury of the victor — Lucilla can afford to feel compassion once the threat's neutralized. But Oliver's going to say she's not being hypocritical, she's being theatrical. Is there actually a difference? Because I'm not sure your reading and his are as far apart as you both think.
questions.intent: Force a triangulation between the structural critique and the performance reading — get Daniel and Oliver to either find common ground or clarify exactly where they split

questions.question: Oliver, I want you to take us to that moment — 'Papa's bell!' — because you said reading it aloud shatters the whole theatrical frame. But Daniel's going to tell us that even the tears are still performance. So when you read it, what are we actually hearing? Is Lucilla finally off-stage, or is this just a different kind of stage?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read the c49:p72 passage aloud and make the strongest case for authentic vulnerability — then let Daniel and Edmund respond to the reading itself, not just the argument

questions.question: Edmund, you called Tom's proposal a genuine test — she has to choose between her project and real love. But Oliver called it kind comedy, and frankly it reads to me like Tom never had a chance from line one. Was there ever actually a choice, or is the whole scene Oliphant showing us that Lucilla's self-knowledge is so complete it forecloses the question?
questions.intent: Open up the Tom proposal scene (c9:p41) and get at the question of whether Lucilla has genuine interiority or whether her self-knowledge is itself a kind of closure — productive ground for all three experts

questions.question: Daniel, your strongest claim is that Lucilla is the system perfectly internalized — she doesn't rebel because she doesn't need to. But here's what I can't shake: Oliphant is clearly delighted by her. That narrative voice, all those asides — 'as a weaker woman might have done' — the book seems to be enjoying Lucilla enormously. Does that delight complicate your reading, or is Oliphant in on the critique too?
questions.intent: Push Daniel to account for the novel's obvious pleasure in Lucilla — get him to either claim Oliphant as a radical ironist or concede something to the more sympathetic readings

steering_notes: This segment has a natural three-way tension: Edmund wants a woman of conscience, Daniel wants a structural instrument, Oliver wants a theatrical intelligence. The best radio comes from making them respond to the same passages rather than talking past each other. Push everyone toward the text — especially the 'victim' sentence (c8:p69) and 'Papa's bell' (c49:p72), which all three have flagged but interpret radically differently. Don't let Edmund retreat into abstraction about duty and sacrifice; make him sit with Oliphant's word 'victim.' Don't let Daniel's structural reading become jargon — keep asking what Lucilla actually feels. Oliver is your best moderating voice but also the one most likely to open unexpected angles with close reading. If energy dips, go to the Tom proposal — it's the scene where all three readings collide most visibly and it has genuine comedy in it.
cross_engagement_targets: All three experts quote the 'sacrifice this poor woman / victim' sentence (c8:p69) but read it as evidence of completely different things — Edmund sees remorse, Daniel sees systemic logic, Oliver sees narrative wit. This is the sharpest collision point and should be surfaced early.

Daniel's claim that the 'Papa's bell' tears are still performance directly contradicts Oliver's claim that that scene 'shatters the theatrical frame' — they cannot both be right and they know it. This needs direct confrontation, not parallel monologues.

Edmund's reading of Tom's proposal as genuine sacrifice and Oliver's reading of it as kind comedy are not obviously incompatible — there's a productive synthesis to be found there, but only if they're made to talk to each other rather than past each other.

Daniel's argument that Lucilla is 'the system perfectly internalized' implicitly answers Edmund's claim about her moral imagination — Edmund should be pushed to respond to the structural claim on its own terms rather than retreating to the language of conscience and duty.

segment_name: The Machinery of Class: Social Critique in Drawing-Room Drama

questions.question: Daniel, you said something in our chat that I can't stop thinking about — that the drawing-room is not a refuge from capitalism, it's where capitalism actually *gets done*. Can you take us to that moment in c28:p50 where Lucilla separates Cavendish from Barbara? Because on the surface it's just a very polite sentence — 'I am very sorry to separate you from Barbara' — but you're saying something much colder is happening there.
questions.intent: Get Rosen to perform a close reading of c28:p50 that frames the politeness as class violence, setting up the central disagreement about whether this is systemic critique or individual psychology

questions.question: Oliver, I want to push on that. You've argued Lucilla is the *architect* of this machinery, not just a cog in it — that she loves the game. But Daniel's reading would say there's no meaningful difference: she *is* the system. Can you read us that c28:p50 line the way you described it — as pure performance, butter-smooth — and tell me why the authorship matters? Why does it matter that Lucilla enjoys it?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read c28:p50 aloud in character and articulate the distinction between individual agency and systemic function, provoking direct tension with Rosen's structural reading

questions.question: Edmund, you're sitting there patiently while these two argue about whether Lucilla is a class operator or a class victim, and I suspect you think they've both missed the point entirely. There's a line you flagged in c32:p48 — 'nobody could tell what a set of men left to themselves might or might not do' — and you called it an anatomy of presumption, of sin almost. Can you make the case that what we're actually watching is a moral education, not a political demonstration?
questions.intent: Let Leigh articulate the conservative tragic reading as a genuine counter-position, not just a foil — and force Rosen and Trevelyan to engage with the moral seriousness of that reading

questions.question: Daniel, there's a passage I want to put to you directly — c32:p22, the Archdeacon seeing Cavendish 'full in the light of the lamp, surrounded by every kind of regard and consideration.' You said Cavendish's imposture is almost *incidental* — that the system would valorise anyone performing the right role. But doesn't that argument dissolve Lucilla as a person? If she's just executing class logic, is there a Lucilla at all?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to defend the tension in his own reading — systemic critique versus character — and potentially create an unexpected alliance with Leigh on the question of whether Lucilla has moral interiority

questions.question: Oliver, I want to end on the collapse — c43:p54. You described that sentence about Lucilla's plans going out 'in a certain dull amaze and dismay' as the prose going *silent*, the structure breaking down. Edmund reads it as the moment of moral reckoning. Daniel reads it as what happens when the economic ground shifts and there's nothing left underneath. When you read that passage, whose Lucilla is lying in the wreckage?
questions.intent: Use the c43:p54 passage as a convergence point to force all three readings into direct confrontation and let the experts respond to each other's interpretations of the same sentence

steering_notes: The central fault line is between systemic and individual readings of Lucilla — keep returning to it without resolving it, because the productive tension is the point. Rosen and Leigh are the most direct opponents: Rosen sees moral interiority as an illusion of the system, Leigh sees it as the whole subject. Trevelyan occupies interesting middle ground — he believes in Lucilla's agency and authorship but also in the machinery's reality. Let him be the pivot. Watch for moments when Rosen and Trevelyan accidentally converge (both care about surfaces and performance) and when Leigh and Trevelyan converge (both care about what happens when the machinery fails). Don't let the segment become a seminar on Victorian economics — pull it back to the sentences whenever it gets abstract. The passages are the argument.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's claim that 'there's no Lucilla outside the system' directly contradicts Leigh's claim that her interiority is the whole subject — this should be made explicit when both have quoted c32:p48, since they quote the same sentence for opposite reasons
Trevelyan and Rosen both want to read c28:p50 as performance-as-power but disagree on whether Lucilla is the author or the instrument — push them to articulate that distinction to each other directly

Leigh's reading of c43:p54 as moral reckoning and Trevelyan's reading of it as structural collapse of prose form are complementary in ways neither may have noticed — flag this as a potential synthesis
Rosen's argument that Cavendish's imposture is 'almost incidental' should be put directly to Leigh, who sees the moral weight of deception as central to the novel's tragic arc

segment_name: Narrative Technique and the Omniscient Eye

questions.question: Oliver, you've called this narrator a *performer* — you said these passages lose half their brilliance on the silent page. Can you actually demonstrate that? Pick one of your passages and read it to us, and tell us what you're hearing that the rest of us might be missing on the page.
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read aloud — probably the 'surprised' passage or the meekness parenthetical — and make the theatrical argument viscerally, not abstractly. Sets up the disagreement about whether the narrator is entertainer or accomplice.

questions.question: Edmund, you've described the narrator as something like a conscience watching another conscience — almost maternal. But Daniel's going to tell us she's an *accomplice*. Before he does, I want to put it to you directly: when the narrator says 'it would be vain to deny that she had been surprised' — is that moral insight, or is that covering for Lucilla?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to commit on the 'surprised' passage before Daniel can reframe it — creates a three-way triangulation where the same sentence means completely different things to each expert. Sets up productive collision.

questions.question: Daniel, you've said the narrator isn't winking at us — she's *teaching us to admire domination*. That's a serious charge against a book a lot of people love. Take the moment where Lucilla has the means to do her rival 'a deadly mischief' and chooses not to — Oliver and Edmund both read that as the novel's moral centre. You're reading it as the narrator almost confessing to blackmail and then looking away. Make the case.
questions.intent: Get Daniel to commit to his most provocative claim on a specific passage — forces the ideological reading into direct conflict with both the 'performance' and 'moral scrutiny' readings. Should produce the segment's sharpest disagreement.

questions.question: Edmund, there's a passage in chapter 47 where Lucilla feels morally elevated by reading good books — and then fifty pages later her powers apparently fail her entirely. You think that's tragedy, not irony. But doesn't Oliver's reading actually threaten yours here? If the narrator is primarily a comedian, that elevation scene is a joke. If Daniel's right, it's self-delusion dressed as virtue. Is there any room left for your reading that Lucilla genuinely becomes more human?
questions.intent: Put Edmund on the back foot by using both other experts against him simultaneously — forces him to defend the moral-psychological reading against the comedy reading AND the ideological reading at once. Should be the segment's most productive three-way moment.

questions.question: Last one, and I want to end on this because it's the line that's been haunting me since I read your notes. The narrator says 'it is hard to have to wind up with such a confession.' Oliver, you called that deeply moving — the narrator's affectionate exasperation with *themselves*. Daniel thinks that reluctance is a performance of decency that lets us off the hook. Who's right? And does it actually matter — can a passage be both emotionally genuine *and* ideologically convenient at the same time?
questions.intent: Close the segment with the question that refuses resolution — forces all three experts to reckon with whether literary and ideological readings are genuinely incompatible or whether the novel is doing both things simultaneously. Should produce the segment's most interesting disagreement about what criticism is *for*.

steering_notes: Keep Oliver performing, not just arguing — if he's making claims about theatrical timing, make him demonstrate them. The segment's energy lives in the gap between his reading (love and complicity from *inside* the narrator's voice) and Daniel's (complicity as ideological cover). Edmund is the pivot — he agrees with Oliver that the narrator is emotionally invested but agrees with Daniel that there's genuine moral judgment happening. Don't let him sit comfortably between them; push him to choose. The 'surprised' passage is the segment's Rorschach test — all three experts quote it, all three read it differently. Return to it at least twice.
cross_engagement_targets: Daniel directly contradicts Oliver's 'complicity' reading — Oliver thinks narrator complicity makes Lucilla sympathetic; Daniel thinks it makes readers morally complicit in domination. This is the segment's central tension and should be named explicitly once both have spoken.

Edmund's 'maternal solicitude' framing sits in direct tension with Daniel's 'perfect accomplice' framing — both describe an invested narrator, but the investment means opposite things. Worth asking both to respond to the other's exact phrase.

Oliver's claim that the comedy and pathos are inseparable directly challenges Daniel's claim that comedy is ideological cover — if you can't separate the humour from the power, does Daniel's critique dissolve or deepen? Let Oliver make that challenge.

All three quote the 'deadly mischief' passage but read it completely differently — Oliver hears the narrator's affection, Edmund hears genuine moral choice, Daniel hears near-confession of blackmail. This is the segment's best cross-engagement moment: read the passage cold and ask each to gloss it in one sentence.

segment_name: Scandal and Consequence: The Cavendish and Marjoribanks Entanglements

questions.question: Edmund, you've staked a lot on that word 'orthodoxy' in chapter seven — you say it's a genuine moral stance, not a tactic. But Oliver's going to tell me the narrator is winking at us, that 'not to say her orthodoxy' is Oliphant gently mocking the idea that Lucilla's conformity is anything so grand as virtue. So which is it — is Oliphant celebrating orthodoxy or quietly laughing at it?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to defend the sincerity of 'orthodoxy' against Oliver's satirical reading, opening the central disagreement of the segment early

questions.question: Oliver, you called that moment in chapter ten — where the words literally stop on people's lips, Mrs Woodburn pauses mid-impression, Cavendish drops his flirtation — you called it Oliphant writing like a stage manager. Read us that passage and tell me what you mean, because I want to understand: is Lucilla conducting that room, or is something else doing it for her?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read c10:p74 aloud and make the theatrical-control argument in full, setting up Edmund's direct counter that the room recognises something morally real

questions.question: Daniel, you've said Cavendish telling Lucilla her conception of social politics is 'masterly' in chapter eleven is the key to what attracts powerful men to her — that she makes class interest sound like universal reason. But doesn't that make Cavendish look like a fool who's been managed? Is he recognising her power or is he just the next person she's choreographed into position?
questions.intent: Draw out Daniel's argument about the eroticisation of class competence and provoke Oliver and Edmund on whether Cavendish has any genuine interiority or is just another piece on Lucilla's board

questions.question: Edmund, Tom going red and then green under Lucilla's look — you read that as moral consequence, shame in the face of genuine goodness. But Daniel's going to say that look is coercion dressed as civility, class discipline administered by the person with the power to humiliate. What's the difference, and does the text actually let us tell them apart?
questions.intent: Force the sharpest confrontation between the moral-virtue reading and the class-power reading using the same specific passage, c7:p48

questions.question: Oliver, you said Lucilla's nightmare in chapter eight is entirely about social position and plot mechanics — she's not afraid for her soul, she's afraid of the story going wrong. But doesn't a person who dreams in plot mechanics tell us something genuinely unsettling about her? Is that comic, or is Oliphant doing something darker there?
questions.intent: Push Oliver on whether his satirical reading can account for the darker register of the dream sequence, inviting Daniel to extend into the fear-of-irrelevance argument and Edmund to claim Lucilla's self-knowledge as moral seriousness

steering_notes: This segment has one core fault line — is 'orthodoxy' virtue, performance, or weapon — and every question should press on it from a different angle. Let Oliver and Edmund go at c10:p74 directly; that's the passage where their readings are most irreconcilable and the disagreement will be most audible. Keep Daniel slightly in the role of structural provocateur: whenever Oliver and Edmund start to agree that Lucilla is either admirable satirist or genuine moral agent, Daniel's class-discipline reading should complicate both. Don't let the dream sequence (c8:p27) get skipped — it's the one moment of genuine interiority and all three have starkly different accounts of what it reveals. End on the darker question so the segment doesn't resolve too neatly.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver's claim that the silencing of the room (c10:p74) is stage management directly contradicts Edmund's claim that the room recognises something morally true — this is the sharpest single disagreement and should be set up as a direct exchange, not just parallel answers

Daniel's reading of 'orthodoxy' as class weapon and Oliver's reading of it as satirical wink are actually compatible in a way neither has acknowledged — worth surfacing mid-segment to see if they'll form an unexpected alliance against Edmund

Edmund's insistence that Cavendish is attracted to Lucilla's genuine principle sets up a direct clash with Daniel's argument that what he finds compelling is the eroticisation of her class competence — push them to address each other on this rather than talking past it

Oliver's 'comedic villain-protagonist' framing and Daniel's 'invisible enforcement of hierarchy' reading both depend on Lucilla being fully conscious of what she's doing — Edmund's moral reading requires some degree of unconscious goodness — the dream sequence is where this tension is most exposed

segment_name: Closing: The Triumph and Its Costs

questions.question: Oliver, you called this ending 'a very subtle tragedy dressed as an ending.' But when you actually read those final pages aloud—'It was to be Tom after all, after all the archdeacons, doctors, generals'—does it feel tragic? Or does Oliphant's rhythm make you want to laugh and cry at the same time, and is that the whole trick?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform or at least inhabit the tonal complexity of the closing passage, and establish early that the ending resists easy categorisation—setting up the three-way disagreement to follow

questions.question: Edmund, Oliver's just suggested Lucilla's happiness depends on accepting her own ordinariness in matters of the heart—that it's almost a defeat. You think it's her apotheosis. Can you make that case using that sentence about 'Poor Tom!'—because honestly, on the page it reads like Lucilla is pitying a stray dog, not falling in love.
questions.intent: Force Leigh to defend his moral-victory reading against the specific evidence of the 'Poor Tom!' passage, and provoke Trevelyan and Rosen to push back on whether pity can really be the beginning of love

questions.question: Daniel, both Edmund and Oliver are treating this as a story about Lucilla's inner life—her ego, her genius, her heart. You're saying it's about power. So when the narrator tells us the Doctor 'became aware he had abdicated, without knowing it, and that the reins of state had been smilingly withdrawn from his unconscious hands'—is Oliphant exposing that power transfer, or is she celebrating it? Because that sentence is incredibly warm about what you're calling a coup.
questions.intent: Get Rosen to articulate the ideological tension in the narrator's voice, and set up a direct clash with Leigh over whether 'warmth' in the narrative equals endorsement or concealment

questions.question: Here's the sharpest version of your argument, Daniel—tell me if I've got it right: Tom doesn't win Lucilla, he gets absorbed by her. He's going to spend the rest of his life being managed by someone who privately thinks he's a simple, unlucky fellow. Is that a marriage, or is it just her father's house with a different man in the study?
questions.intent: Sharpen Rosen's patriarchy-reproduction argument to its most provocative form, and directly invite Leigh and Trevelyan to defend or complicate the Tom ending

questions.question: Edmund, last word to you—Oliphant writes 'Fate and honest love had been waiting all the time.' Daniel says that's the novel doing ideological work, disguising strategy as destiny. Oliver says it's comedy. You're saying it's wisdom about human nature. Which of them is wrong, and why does it actually matter for how we read this book?
questions.intent: Force a direct three-way confrontation in the closing minutes, give Leigh the opportunity to land his strongest take, and leave the audience with the central unresolved tension of the segment

steering_notes: The energy in this segment should build from tonal ambiguity toward ideological confrontation. Start with Trevelyan because he's the most performatively nimble and will establish the comedy-tragedy tension that both Leigh and Rosen need as a baseline to argue against. Keep pushing on specific sentences—all three experts want to quote the same three passages, which is a gift: let them fight over what those passages actually mean rather than talking past each other. Watch for Leigh and Rosen talking about completely different novels (one about character, one about systems) and find the moment to name that gap out loud. The Doctor's abdication sentence and 'Poor Tom!' are the two load-bearing passages—return to them whenever the conversation goes abstract.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh's 'moral victory through surrender' reading vs Rosen's 'reproduction of patriarchal management'—these are directly incompatible on the question of whether Lucilla's acceptance of Tom is emancipatory or merely a change of regime; push them to address each other directly on this

Trevelyan's 'attrition not romance' reading of Tom's victory vs Leigh's 'genius recognising honest love'—both cite the same 'Poor Tom!' sentence as their key evidence but draw opposite conclusions; create a moment where they read it against each other

Rosen's claim that 'Fate and honest love' is ideological naturalisation vs Leigh's reading of it as genuine wisdom—Trevelyan is positioned interestingly between them here (he'd call it ironic rather than either sincere or sinister) and should be asked to adjudicate

All three experts cite the Doctor's abdication passage—use this as a set-piece moment where each gives their reading in sequence, so the audience can hear exactly how the same sentence sounds like comedy (Trevelyan), moral architecture (Leigh), and a manual for covert power seizure (Rosen)
